finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the dba role check is never enforced. Any request that reaches the handler with a user in its context can run the DROP TABLE.
finding.source: Any HTTP client able to reach POST/GET /admin/drop on :8083, authenticated as a user without the 'dba' role.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered to dropTable and served on :8083 (api.go:46) with no middleware.
userFrom(r) loads the user from the request context.
Authorize(u, "dba") returns errors.New("forbidden") for non-dba users, but the return value is discarded.
Execution continues to runSQL regardless of the authorization result.
Contrast: vacuum checks the error and returns 403, so the missing check in dropTable is a defect.

finding.guards_checked: Authorize error is not checked in dropTable. No auth middleware wraps the handler: http.HandleFunc is called directly on the default mux. The only other guard is the context user, which is not set anywhere in this file. Even if upstream code sets it, the role check is the only authorization control.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize (api.go:13-20) returns an error for non-dba users, but dropTable discards it at api.go:26. The only other guard is the unchecked type assertion in userFrom (api.go:22), which panics if no user is in the context. net/http recovers that panic, so it only blocks requests with no user. There is no middleware, because main serves the default mux directly (api.go:44-46).
verdict.reason: api.go:26 calls Authorize as a bare statement and drops its "forbidden" error, so a non-dba user with a context user reaches runSQL("DROP TABLE "+r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27, while vacuum checks the error at api.go:33. Caveat: this file never sets the context user, so the attacker must be authenticated through some upstream code that is not in this file.

finding.claim: SQL injection: the form value 't' is concatenated straight into a DROP TABLE statement. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, for example by adding extra statements or targeting any table.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t") on /admin/drop, which reads query-string and body parameters and is attacker-controlled.

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the SQL string with no validation, allowlist or identifier quoting.
runSQL is a stub here. A real implementation would execute the string, and DDL identifiers cannot be parameterized, so an allowlist is needed.

finding.guards_checked: No identifier allowlist, regex validation, or quoting. The only guard is the dba role check, which is not enforced (see AUTH-1). Even a correctly enforced check would leave the injection open to any dba. runSQL is an empty stub in this repo, so the exact impact depends on the real implementation.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded as a bare statement, so it blocks nothing. There is no allowlist, quoting or parameterization on the 't' value.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates the unvalidated r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE ...", and the only guard, Authorize at api.go:26, has its error ignored (compare the correct check at api.go:33), so any caller who reaches the handler can inject SQL. The impact assumes a real runSQL, since the stub at api.go:41 does nothing.

finding.claim: userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the context value. If no auth middleware has set 'user', the assertion panics and every admin request fails. If the value is a different type, it also panics. This is a robustness and fail-open concern rather than a direct bypass. Authentication is not enforced anywhere in this code.

trace.note: Routes are registered without any authentication middleware.
The context value is asserted as *User without a comma-ok check. A missing value panics, and net/http recovers it per connection.

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware exists in the repo, and nothing in api.go sets the 'user' context key. A plain string context key is also collision-prone. Impact is limited to a panic and denial of a single request, so this is low severity. It matters mainly if upstream middleware is absent in deployment.

verdict.guard_found: None in the repo: there is no auth middleware, and api.go sets no "user" context key. The unchecked assertion at api.go:22 panics before any handler effect runs, so it acts as an accidental fail-closed barrier. net/http recovers the panic per request.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (api.go:22 is an unchecked assertion, api.go:44-45 register routes with no middleware, and api.go:25 and :32 call userFrom first), but the panic at api.go:22 happens before runSQL at api.go:27 or :37, so it fails closed. The result is only an aborted request that net/http recovers, with no security impact; the claim itself concedes it is not a bypass. The real flaw, the discarded Authorize result at api.go:26, is a separate finding.
